outcome.answer: Language-model representations track human sentence-processing effort, but the best-matching layers depend on the task. For naturalistic reading, earlier layers align better with human behavior; for syntactically ambiguous, challenging sentences, later layers estimate effort better, though they still underestimate it [1]. LM surprisal also predicts reading times, and tracking long-range coreference improves its fit to human reading behavior [4]. Other model-derived measures, including information-theoretic storage cost and energy, predict reading-time variation beyond standard predictors [5, 9]. These findings concern behavioral effort and reading time; the supplied papers do not establish a single, universal correspondence between internal representations and human effort.
